```{r setup}
#| include: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(psych)
library(vegan)
library(emmeans)
library(corrplot)
library(factoextra)
library(ggrepel)
library(patchwork)
library(tidyverse)
library(GGally)

# Permutation tests resample at random. Fixing the seed means the numbers on
# these slides are the numbers you get when you run the code yourself.
set.seed(42)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 9))

# ---- Dataset 1: Darlingtonia morphology (continuous, one unit per column) ----
darlingtonia <- read_csv("data/darlingtonia.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

darl_numeric <- darlingtonia %>% dplyr::select(-site)
darl_scaled  <- scale(darl_numeric)

# ---- Dataset 2: Doubs River fish (species counts, lots of zeros) ----
doubs_spe <- read_csv("data/DoubsSpe.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  rename(site = 1)
doubs_env <- read_csv("data/DoubsEnv.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  rename(site = 1) %>%
  mutate(reach = factor(
    case_when(das <  100 ~ "Upstream",
              das <  250 ~ "Midstream",
              TRUE       ~ "Downstream"),
    levels = c("Upstream", "Midstream", "Downstream")))

doubs_mat <- as.matrix(doubs_spe %>% dplyr::select(-site))
```

## Part 1 · Why Multivariate Data? {.divider}

## Where We Have Been

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
### One response variable at a time

- Everything from *t*-tests through ANCOVA and mixed models shared one structure:
  - **One** response variable, *y*
  - One or more predictors
  - Partition the variance in *y*
- That works when the biology really is about one number — lifespan, mass, count, survival.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
### But ecology is rarely one number

- A plant is its **whole shape**: height *and* mouth *and* tube *and* wing *and* mass.
- A stream site is its **whole fish community**: 27 species at once.
- Running 10 separate ANOVAs on 10 traits:
  - inflates the family-wise error rate,
  - and still never tells you how the traits **go together**.
:::
:::::

## Introduction to Multivariate Analysis

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
### What multivariate methods do

- Take many correlated variables measured on the same objects and ask:
  - Which objects **resemble** which?
  - What are the main **axes of variation**?
  - Do **groups** differ in their overall multivariate makeup?
- Three jobs, in order, and this lecture is a map of all three:
  1.  Put variables on a common footing — **standardization**
  2.  Turn objects into resemblances — **distance / dissimilarity**
  3.  Draw the resemblances in 2-D — **ordination**

::: callout-note
Gotelli & Ellison, *A Primer of Ecological Statistics*, Ch. 12 — The Analysis of Multivariate Data — is the core reference for this lecture.
:::
::::

::: {.column width="40%"}
*Darlingtonia californica* (cobra lily)

![Photo of a cobra lily (Darlingtonia californica) showing its hooded, pitcher-shaped leaves and forked, tongue-like appendages, the carnivorous plant whose morphology this lecture's PCA example analyzes.](images/clipboard-3752708543.png){width="3.20in"}
:::
::::::

## Our First Dataset: Darlingtonia

::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
### Cobra lily morphology

- `r nrow(darlingtonia)` plants from **4 sites** in the Siskiyou Mountains of Oregon, **10 variables** each.
- **Morphology (mm)**: `height`, `mouth_diam`, `tube_diam`, `keel_diam`, `wing1_length`, `wing2_length`, `wingsprea`
- **Biomass (g)**: `hoodmass_g`, `tubemass_g`, `wingmass_g`
- **Sites**: TJH (T.J. Howell's Fen) · DG (Day's Gulch) · LEH (L.E. Hunter's Fen) · HD (High Divide)

```{r site_counts}
#| echo: false
darlingtonia %>% count(site, name = "n_plants")
```
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
*Pitcher structure showing the measured features*

![Vintage-style line illustration of three Darlingtonia pitcher-leaf structures with their hooded tops, tube bodies, and forked wing appendages labeled by shape, showing the plant parts behind variables like height, mouth diameter, tube diameter, and wing length/spread used in the PCA.](images/clipboard-4005369252.png){width="2.00in"}

- All **continuous**, all **positive**, mostly **correlated** — the classic setting for PCA.
:::
:::::

## Our Second Dataset: Doubs River Fish

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
### A very different kind of multivariate data

- `r nrow(doubs_spe)` sites along the Doubs River (France), `r ncol(doubs_spe) - 1` fish species, **abundance counts**.
- Sites are ordered **upstream → downstream**, so there is a real environmental gradient to recover.
- The structural difference that matters:
  - **`r round(100 * mean(doubs_mat == 0), 1)`% of the entries are zeros.**
  - Species richness ranges from `r min(rowSums(doubs_mat > 0))` to `r max(rowSums(doubs_mat > 0))` species per site.
- Count data, shared absences, wildly different totals. This is why Euclidean distance is **not** always the right answer.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r doubs_peek}
#| echo: false
doubs_spe %>%
  dplyr::select(site, CHA, TRU, VAI, LOC, GAR, ABL) %>%
  slice(c(1, 2, 14, 15, 28, 29))
```

- Site 1 holds a **single** species (3 brown trout).
- Site 29 holds **26**.
- Nothing in a *t*-test or an ANOVA handles a response like this.
:::
:::::

```{r load_show}
#| echo: true

darlingtonia <- read_csv("data/darlingtonia.csv")

```

## Exploring the Raw Darlingtonia Data

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
### Always look first

- Check for outliers, examine distributions, look for patterns by site, understand the **scales**.
- **Key observations**:
  - Variables measured in different units (mm vs. g)
  - Height is in the **hundreds**; wing mass is in **hundredths**
  - We will have to standardize before we can combine them
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r explore_data}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4.2
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-alt: "Faceted boxplots of each of the 10 raw Darlingtonia morphology and biomass variables by collection site, each panel on its own free y-axis scale, showing the variables have very different ranges."

darlingtonia %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -site, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = site, y = value, fill = site)) +
  geom_boxplot(linewidth = 0.3, outlier.size = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 6) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Raw data by site — notice the different scales",
       x = NULL, y = NULL)
```
:::
:::::

## Part 2 · Standardization {.divider}

## The Problem of Different Scales

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
### Why standardization matters

- Variables with larger numbers dominate any distance you compute.
- **In this data**:

```{r scale_problem}
#| echo: false
darlingtonia %>%
  summarize(sd_height   = sd(height),
            sd_wingmass = sd(wingmass_g),
            ratio       = sd(height) / sd(wingmass_g)) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

- Height varies about **990×** more than wing mass does. In a raw Euclidean distance, wing mass contributes essentially nothing.
- That is an accident of **units**, not biology.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
### Z-score standardization

- $Z = \dfrac{Y_i - \bar{Y}}{s}$
- Each variable becomes:
  - Mean = 0
  - Standard deviation = 1
  - Units = "standard deviations from the mean"
- Every variable now gets an **equal vote**.

```{r standardize_code}
#| echo: true
darl_numeric <- darlingtonia %>%
  dplyr::select(-site)

darl_scaled <- scale(darl_numeric)
```
:::
:::::

## Standardization in Pictures

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r scaled_comparison}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4.0
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-alt: "Two stacked panels of boxplots by site for height and mouth diameter: raw values on different scales on top, and standardized z-scored values on a common scale below, showing standardization equalizes the variables' influence."

p1 <- darlingtonia %>%
  dplyr::select(site, height, mouth_diam) %>%
  pivot_longer(-site, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = site, y = value, fill = site)) +
  geom_boxplot(linewidth = 0.3, outlier.size = 0.5) +
  facet_grid(variable ~ ., scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Raw data (different scales)", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 7) + theme(legend.position = "none")

p2 <- as.data.frame(darl_scaled) %>%
  mutate(site = darlingtonia$site) %>%
  dplyr::select(site, height, mouth_diam) %>%
  pivot_longer(-site, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = site, y = value, fill = site)) +
  geom_boxplot(linewidth = 0.3, outlier.size = 0.5) +
  facet_grid(variable ~ ., scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Standardized (same scale)", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 7) + theme(legend.position = "none")

p1 / p2
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### When *not* to standardize

- **Same units, and the differences in spread are real biology.**
  - Ten lengths all in mm, where "this trait varies more" is the finding — standardizing would erase it.
- **Species abundance data.** Standardizing each species to mean 0 turns absences into negative numbers, and most dissimilarity measures for community data are undefined for negatives.
  - Community data gets **transformed** (square-root, Hellinger) rather than z-scored. More on that in week 15.
- The question to ask is always: *do I want these variables to have equal influence?*
:::
:::::

## Part 3 · Distance and Dissimilarity {.divider}

## Euclidean Distance Between Two Objects

::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
### How different are two plants?

- **Two variables** (height, mouth diameter):
  - $d_{i,j} = \sqrt{(y_{i,1} - y_{j,1})^2 + (y_{i,2} - y_{j,2})^2}$
- **p variables**:
  - $d_{i,j} = \sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^{p}(y_{i,k} - y_{j,k})^2}$
- The Pythagorean theorem, extended to as many dimensions as you have variables.
- **Always compute it on standardized values** — otherwise you are measuring your unit choices, not your plants.
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
```{r distance_example}
#| echo: true
# distance between plants 1 and 2
# on the STANDARDIZED data
z <- scale(darl_numeric)

round(sqrt(sum((z[1, ] - z[2, ])^2)), 2)

# same thing, via dist()
round(as.matrix(dist(z))[1, 2], 2)
```

- `r round(as.matrix(dist(scale(darl_numeric)))[1,2], 2)` **standard deviations** apart across all 10 traits.
:::
:::::

## The Dissimilarity Matrix

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
### The hub of everything that follows

- `dist()` returns one number for **every pair** of objects: an *n* × *n* **dissimilarity matrix**.
- With `r nrow(darlingtonia)` plants that is `r format(nrow(darlingtonia) * (nrow(darlingtonia) - 1) / 2, big.mark = ",")` pairwise distances.
- **Why it matters**: PCoA, NMDS, cluster analysis, PERMANOVA and ANOSIM *all* start from this matrix and nothing else.
  - Choose the metric well and everything downstream is sensible.
  - Choose it badly and no amount of clever plotting rescues you.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r dist_matrix_peek}
#| echo: true
d_darl <- dist(z)          # Euclidean

# the corner of the matrix
round(as.matrix(d_darl)[1:5, 1:5], 2)
```

- Symmetric, zero on the diagonal, and that is all an ordination method ever sees.
:::
:::::

## Not All Distances Are Euclidean

### Four metrics you will meet in this course

::: compact-table
| Metric | Formula idea | Data it suits | Range |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| **Euclidean** | straight-line distance | continuous, standardized, few zeros | 0 → ∞ |
| **Manhattan** | sum of absolute differences | continuous, less outlier-sensitive | 0 → ∞ |
| **Bray–Curtis** | shared abundance / total abundance | species abundance counts | 0 → 1 |
| **Jaccard** | shared species / total species | presence–absence | 0 → 1 |
:::

- Euclidean and Manhattan are **metric** distances — they obey the triangle inequality and can be drawn in a real coordinate space.
- Bray–Curtis and Jaccard are **semi-metric dissimilarities** — bounded at 1 (= "share nothing"), which is exactly what you want for communities, but which breaks the geometry PCA relies on.

## The Double-Zero Problem

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
### Why community data needs Bray–Curtis

- Doubs site 1 holds **one** species. Site 29 holds **26**. They share **nothing**.
- Euclidean distance counts all the species that are absent from *both* sites as **evidence of similarity** — two barren sites look like twins.
- Ecologically that is nonsense: a species can be absent for a dozen unrelated reasons.
- **Bray–Curtis ignores double zeros entirely** and returns 1 for two sites with nothing in common.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r double_zero}
#| echo: true
# sites 1 and 29 share no species
e <- as.matrix(vegdist(doubs_mat,
                       method = "euclidean"))
b <- as.matrix(vegdist(doubs_mat,
                       method = "bray"))

c(euclidean = round(e[1, 29], 2),
  bray      = round(b[1, 29], 3))
```

- Bray–Curtis says **1.0 — maximally different**, which is correct.
- Euclidean returns a number with no upper bound and no interpretation.
:::
:::::

## Choosing a Distance Metric

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Decision rules

- **Continuous traits, environmental variables, few zeros**
  - → standardize, then **Euclidean**
  - → PCA is available to you
- **Species abundances with many zeros**
  - → transform, then **Bray–Curtis**
  - → PCA is *not* appropriate; use NMDS or PCoA
- **Presence–absence**
  - → **Jaccard** (or Sørensen)
- **Outlier-heavy continuous data**
  - → **Manhattan**, which does not square the differences
:::

:::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r metric_compare}
#| echo: true
# same data, three metrics, first pair
round(c(
  euclidean = vegdist(doubs_mat,
                 method = "euclidean")[1],
  manhattan = vegdist(doubs_mat,
                 method = "manhattan")[1],
  bray      = vegdist(doubs_mat,
                 method = "bray")[1],
  jaccard   = vegdist(doubs_mat > 0,
                 method = "jaccard")[1]), 3)
```

::: callout-important
The metric is a **modelling decision**, not a default. It encodes what you mean by "different".
:::
::::
::::::

## Part 4 · Ordination — The Big Picture {.divider}

## What Ordination Does

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
### Many dimensions → a readable map

- You have `r ncol(darl_numeric)` variables, so each plant is a point in **`r ncol(darl_numeric)`-dimensional space**. Nobody can see that.
- **Ordination** finds a 2-D (or 3-D) map in which objects that were close in the full space are still close on the page.
- It is a **lossy** summary. Some information is always thrown away; the honest report always says **how much**.
- The word means "putting in order" — arranging objects along axes.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
![Scatterplot of a correlated two-variable Gaussian point cloud with two perpendicular black arrows overlaid, the longer arrow pointing along the direction of greatest spread (the first principal axis) and the shorter arrow perpendicular to it (the second), illustrating how PCA finds new axes aligned with the directions of maximum variance.](images/clipboard-2517015273.png){width="2.56in"}

Reducing 2 variables to 1 principal axis: the new axis points along the direction of greatest spread.
:::
:::::

## The Map of Ordination Methods

::: compact-table
| Method | Starts from | Distance implied | How it solves | Where in this course |
|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| **PCA** | raw / standardized variables | Euclidean only | eigen-decomposition | **Week 14** |
| **PCoA** | *any* dissimilarity matrix | whatever you chose | eigen-decomposition | named only |
| **CA / DCA** | species count table | chi-square | eigen-decomposition | named only |
| **NMDS** | *any* dissimilarity matrix | whatever you chose | iterative, rank-based | **Week 15** |
| **Cluster** | *any* dissimilarity matrix | whatever you chose | agglomerative joining | **Week 15** |
:::

- The top block is **eigenanalysis**: one exact answer, axes ranked by variance explained, and you can read loadings off them.
- **NMDS is different**: it preserves only the *rank order* of the dissimilarities, solves by iteration, and has no "% variance explained" — it has **stress** instead.
- **Cluster analysis** answers a different question entirely: not "where does each object sit?" but "which objects group together?"

## Eigenanalysis vs. Iteration

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Eigen methods (PCA, PCoA, CA)

- Find axes by **decomposing** the correlation or distance structure directly.
- Give you:
  - an **exact, reproducible** answer
  - axes **ordered** by variance explained
  - **loadings**: how each variable builds each axis
- But they assume the distance is **Euclidean-like** and the relationships are **linear**.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### NMDS

- Does not decompose anything. It **searches**: shuffle the points, measure how badly the map distorts the rank order of distances, repeat.
- Gives you:
  - a map honouring **any** dissimilarity you like
  - no linearity assumption
  - **stress** as the goodness-of-fit
- But: no loadings, axes are **arbitrary**, and a different random start can give a rotated answer.
:::
:::::

## Part 5 · A First Ordination — PCA {.divider}

## PCA in One Slide

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
### The idea

- PCA builds new variables (**components**) that are:
  - **Linear combinations** of the original variables
  - **Uncorrelated** with each other
  - **Ordered** by how much variance they capture
- For plant *i* on component *k*:
  - $Z_{ik} = a_{k1}Y_{i1} + a_{k2}Y_{i2} + \ldots + a_{kp}Y_{ip}$
  - $a_{kj}$ = the **loading** of variable *j* on component *k*
  - $Z_{ik}$ = the **score** of plant *i* on component *k*
- PC1 takes as much variance as any single axis can; PC2 takes as much of what is left as possible, at right angles to PC1; and so on.
:::

:::: {.column width="45%"}
### Running it

```{r run_pca}
#| echo: true
pca_result <- prcomp(darl_numeric,
                     center = TRUE,
                     scale. = TRUE)
```

- `center = TRUE` → mean 0
- `scale. = TRUE` → SD 1 (note the **dot**)
- Together those two arguments are the standardization from Part 2.

::: callout-note
**Next week** we open the box: eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and what `prcomp()` is actually solving.
:::
::::
::::::

## Do the Variables Even Correlate?

::::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
### PCA only helps if they do

- PCA earns its keep by **collapsing redundancy**. If the variables are already uncorrelated, there is no redundancy to collapse and the components are just the original variables, reordered.
- Here the strongest pairs are:

```{r cor_top}
#| echo: false
cm <- cor(darl_numeric)
as_tibble(as.table(cm), .name_repair = "unique") %>%
  setNames(c("v1", "v2", "r")) %>%
  filter(v1 < v2) %>%
  slice_max(abs(r), n = 4) %>%
  transmute(pair = paste(v1, "~", v2), r = round(r, 3))
```
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r correlation_plot}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 3.8
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-alt: "Correlation matrix heatmap of the 10 Darlingtonia morphology and biomass variables, colored and hierarchically clustered, with correlation coefficients printed in each cell, showing several strongly correlated variable clusters."

ggpairs(darl_numeric)
# corrplot(cor(darl_numeric), method = "color", type = "upper",
#          order = "hclust", tl.col = "black", tl.cex = 0.65,
#          addCoef.col = "black", number.cex = 0.5, mar = c(0, 0, 1, 0))
```
:::
:::::

## How Much Did We Capture?

::::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Variance explained

```{r variance_explained}
#| echo: false
ev       <- pca_result$sdev^2
prop_var <- ev / sum(ev)

tibble(PC         = paste0("PC", 1:length(ev)),
       Eigenvalue = round(ev, 3),
       Percent    = round(prop_var * 100, 1),
       Cumulative = round(cumsum(prop_var) * 100, 1)) %>%
  head(6)
```

- PC1 = **`r round(prop_var[1]*100, 1)`%**, PC2 = **`r round(prop_var[2]*100, 1)`%**, PC3 = **`r round(prop_var[3]*100, 1)`%**
- First three together: **`r round(sum(prop_var[1:3])*100, 1)`%** of all variation in 10 variables, in 3 numbers.
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r scree_plot}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 3.8
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-alt: "Scree plot of percentage variance explained by each of the 10 principal components as blue bars, with a red cumulative-variance line and a dashed reference line at 70%, showing the first three components already exceed that threshold."

tibble(PC = factor(1:length(ev)),
       Variance = prop_var * 100,
       Cumulative = cumsum(prop_var) * 100) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = PC)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = Variance), fill = "darkblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Cumulative, group = 1), color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(y = Cumulative), color = "red", size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 70, linetype = "dashed", color = "darkgray") +
  annotate("text", x = 8, y = 76, label = "70%", color = "darkgray", size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Scree plot", subtitle = "Bars = each PC, line = cumulative",
       x = "Principal component", y = "% variance explained") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8)
```

- The **elbow** after PC3 is the usual cue to stop.
:::
:::::

## Reading the Loadings

::::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
### What loads where

```{r loadings_table}
#| echo: false
round(pca_result$rotation[, 1:3], 3)
```
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
### Rules of thumb

- Loadings beyond **±0.3** are worth discussing; beyond **±0.5** they dominate the axis.
- Near zero means the variable has nothing to say about that axis.
- **PC1**: nearly every variable loads in the **same direction** with similar magnitude → a general **size** axis.
- **PC2**: `tube_diam` and `keel_diam` stand apart from the rest → **tube girth**.
- **PC3**: `wingsprea` and `wing2_length` dominate → a **wing** axis.
:::
:::::

## ⚠️ The Sign of a Component Is Arbitrary

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
### This trips up every student once

- On this run, **every PC1 loading is negative**. Run the same code on a different machine, or drop one plant, and they may all come back positive.
- **Both answers are equally correct.** An eigenvector defines a *line*, and a line has no preferred end. Multiplying a whole component — loadings **and** scores — by −1 changes nothing:
  - the variance explained is identical
  - the distances between points are identical
  - the biology is identical
- What you must **never** do is flip the loadings and not the scores.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r sign_demo}
#| echo: true
# PC1 loadings are all negative here,
# so a HIGH PC1 score = a SMALL plant
round(pca_result$rotation[1:4, 1], 3)

# flipping is legal and changes nothing
flip <- -pca_result$x[, 1]
round(c(var_original = var(pca_result$x[, 1]),
        var_flipped  = var(flip)), 3)
```

**Always check the sign before you write a sentence** such as "site X has higher PC1". Say what it means biologically, not just which way the number went.
:::
:::::

## PC1: A Size Axis

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r pc1_loading_plot}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 3.8
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart of PC1 loadings for each of the 10 variables, colored by sign, showing most variables loading in the same (negative) direction and only keel and tube diameter opposing them, consistent with PC1 representing overall plant size."

tibble(Variable = rownames(pca_result$rotation),
       Loading  = pca_result$rotation[, 1]) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(Variable, Loading), y = Loading)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = Loading > 0), show.legend = FALSE) +
  coord_flip() + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "darkblue", "TRUE" = "coral")) +
  labs(title = "PC1 loadings", subtitle = "Overall plant size",
       x = NULL, y = "Loading") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Interpretation

- Eight of ten variables load together between about **−0.24 and −0.39**: height, mouth, both wings, wing spread, and all three masses.
- Only `keel_diam` (**`r round(pca_result$rotation["keel_diam", 1], 3)`**) and `tube_diam` (**`r round(pca_result$rotation["tube_diam", 1], 3)`**) sit apart.
- **Biological meaning**: bigger plants are bigger in nearly every way. PC1 is **general size**.
- Because the loadings are negative on this run:
  - **low PC1 score → large plant**
  - **high PC1 score → small plant**
:::
:::::

## PC2 and PC3: Shape Axes

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r pc2_pc3_plot}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4.0
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-alt: "Two horizontal bar charts of loadings side by side: PC2 dominated by tube diameter and keel diameter, and PC3 dominated by wing spread and wing length, showing the two shape axes."

mk <- function(k, ttl, sub) {
  tibble(Variable = rownames(pca_result$rotation),
         Loading  = pca_result$rotation[, k]) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = reorder(Variable, Loading), y = Loading)) +
    geom_col(aes(fill = Loading > 0), show.legend = FALSE) +
    coord_flip() + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "darkblue", "TRUE" = "coral")) +
    labs(title = ttl, subtitle = sub, x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 7)
}
mk(2, "PC2", "Tube girth") | mk(3, "PC3", "Wings")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### What these axes are

- **PC2 (`r round(prop_var[2]*100, 1)`%) — tube girth.** `tube_diam` (`r round(pca_result$rotation["tube_diam", 2], 2)`) and `keel_diam` (`r round(pca_result$rotation["keel_diam", 2], 2)`) dominate, with height also loading. A plant can be tall and thin-tubed, or short and fat-tubed, at any overall size.
- **PC3 (`r round(prop_var[3]*100, 1)`%) — wings.** `wingsprea` (`r round(pca_result$rotation["wingsprea", 3], 2)`) and `wing2_length` (`r round(pca_result$rotation["wing2_length", 3], 2)`) dominate. How far the trap's forked appendages spread, independent of size and tube girth.
- This is PCA doing its job: three **independent** descriptions of shape, out of ten entangled measurements.
:::
:::::

## Scores: Putting the Plants on the Map

::::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
### What scores are

- A **score** is one plant's value on one component — its coordinate in the new space.
- `pca_result$x` holds them, one row per plant.

```{r pc_scores}
#| echo: false
pc_scores <- as_tibble(pca_result$x) %>%
  mutate(site = darlingtonia$site, plant_id = 1:n())

pc_scores %>%
  dplyr::select(plant_id, site, PC1, PC2, PC3) %>%
  head(6) %>%
  mutate(across(PC1:PC3, \(x) round(x, 2)))
```
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r scores_plot}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 3.8
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of PC1 versus PC2 scores for each plant, colored by site with 68% confidence ellipses, showing partial separation between sites in the size-girth plane."

ggplot(pc_scores, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = site)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  stat_ellipse(level = 0.68, linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "PCA scores",
       x = paste0("PC1: size (", round(prop_var[1]*100, 1), "%)"),
       y = paste0("PC2: tube girth (", round(prop_var[2]*100, 1), "%)"),
       color = "Site") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8)
```

- This is an **ordination**: plants ordered along interpretable axes.
:::
:::::

## The Biplot

::::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Reading it

- **Points** = plants (scores). **Arrows** = variables (loadings).
- **Arrow length** = how strongly that variable is represented in this plane.
- **Angle between arrows** = correlation: small angle → positively correlated; 90° → uncorrelated; 180° → negatively correlated.
- A plant lying out along an arrow is **high** in that variable.
- **HD plants sit to the right** — and because PC1 loadings are negative, right means **small**. HD grows the smallest plants.
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r biplot}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 3.8
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-alt: "PCA biplot of PC1 and PC2 with plants as points colored by site with confidence ellipses, and arrows for each original variable showing its loading direction and strength."

fviz_pca_biplot(pca_result, geom.ind = "point",
                col.ind = darlingtonia$site,
                palette = c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#CC79A7"),
                addEllipses = TRUE, label = "var",
                col.var = "black", repel = TRUE, labelsize = 2.5,
                title = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 7) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
:::
:::::

## Part 6 · A First NMDS {.divider}

## Why the Fish Data Needs a Different Tool

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
### PCA would be the wrong choice here

- `r round(100 * mean(doubs_mat == 0), 1)`% zeros, counts spanning orders of magnitude, and a strong **non-linear** gradient from headwater to lowland.
- PCA would impose Euclidean distance, treat shared absences as similarity, and spread the sites along a meaningless horseshoe.
- **NMDS instead**:
  1.  Compute Bray–Curtis dissimilarities.
  2.  Drop the sites onto a 2-D map at random.
  3.  Nudge them until the **rank order** of map distances matches the rank order of real dissimilarities as closely as possible.
  4.  Report **stress** — how badly it still fails.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r nmds_run}
#| echo: true
#| results: hide
#| message: false
nmds <- metaMDS(doubs_mat,
                distance = "bray",
                k = 2, trymax = 50,
                trace = 0)
```

```{r nmds_stress}
#| echo: true
round(nmds$stress, 3)
```

- **Stress rules of thumb**: \< 0.05 excellent · \< 0.1 good · \< 0.2 usable · \> 0.3 meaningless.
:::
:::::

## The NMDS Map

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r nmds_plot}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4.0
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-alt: "NMDS ordination of the 29 Doubs River sites in two dimensions, points colored by river reach with 68% ellipses and labeled by site number, showing upstream, midstream, and downstream sites separating along a gradient."

as_tibble(scores(nmds, display = "sites")) %>%
  mutate(site  = doubs_spe$site
         # ,
         # reach = doubs_env$reach
        ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(NMDS1, NMDS2, color = site)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = site), size = 2.2, show.legend = FALSE) +
  stat_ellipse(level = 0.68, linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(title = paste0("Doubs fish, Bray-Curtis NMDS (stress = ",
                      round(nmds$stress, 3), ")"),
       color = "Reach") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
:::

:::: {.column width="48%"}
### What to notice

- Sites arrange along a **gradient**, in roughly their real upstream-to-downstream order — which NMDS was never told.
- Stress = **`r round(nmds$stress, 3)`**: a good 2-D fit.
- **The axes mean nothing.** No variance explained, no loadings; the map can be rotated or reflected freely.
- Contrast the PCA biplot, whose axes carried percentages and whose arrows carried meaning.

::: callout-note
Week 15 takes this apart properly: the algorithm, Shepard diagrams, choosing *k*, and fitting environmental vectors.
:::
::::
::::::

## Part 7 · Testing Group Differences {.divider}

## Do the Sites Actually Differ?

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Route 1 — ANOVA on component scores

- PC scores are ordinary continuous variables, and they are **uncorrelated** with one another by construction — so you may put them straight into the ANOVA you already know.
- One test per component, each answering a different question about shape.

```{r anova_pcs}
#| echo: true
#| class-output: tight-code
map_dfr(c("PC1", "PC2", "PC3"), \(k) {
  a <- summary(aov(pc_scores[[k]] ~ pc_scores$site))[[1]]
  tibble(PC = k, F = round(a[1, 4], 2),
         p = signif(a[1, 5], 3))
})
```
:::

:::: {.column width="50%"}
### What it says

- **All three** components differ significantly among sites.
- Sites differ in **size** (PC1), in **tube girth** (PC2) *and* in **wing spread** (PC3) — the sites are not simply scaled versions of one another.
- **The caveat**: this is three tests on three axes chosen by the data themselves. It is a reasonable *description*, not a clean confirmatory test.

::: callout-warning
PCA was run on all `r nrow(darlingtonia)` plants at once, ignoring site. The components are therefore not independent of the grouping you then test. Treat these *p*-values as exploratory.
:::
::::
::::::

## Which Sites Differ, and How?

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r posthoc}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| class-output: tight-code
pc1_emm <- emmeans(aov(PC1 ~ site, data = pc_scores), ~ site)
multcomp::cld(pc1_emm, Letters = letters)
```
:::

:::: {.column width="48%"}
### Reading it in biology, not in numbers

- **HD** sits alone in its own group with the **highest** PC1 score.
- PC1 loadings are negative, so a high score means a **small** plant: **HD grows the smallest cobra lilies**, and significantly so.
- DG sits at the other end — the **largest** plants.
- LEH and TJH overlap in the middle.

::: callout-important
This is the sign trap in action. "HD has the highest PC1" and "HD has the smallest plants" are the **same sentence**. Always translate before you write.
:::
::::
::::::

## Route 2 — PERMANOVA on the Distance Matrix {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Test the whole community at once

- PERMANOVA skips the ordination entirely: it partitions the **dissimilarity matrix** directly and gets its *p*-value by **permuting group labels**.
- One test on all `r ncol(darl_numeric)` variables at once, instead of one per component.

```{r permanova}
#| echo: true
#| class-output: tight-code
adonis2(darl_scaled ~ site,
        data   = darlingtonia,
        method = "euclidean")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Why it is worth knowing now

- No normality assumption, no multivariate normality, no equal covariance matrices.
- Works on **any** dissimilarity you can justify — which is why it is the natural partner to NMDS.
- `R2` is the fraction of total dissimilarity attributable to site — read it like an ANOVA's $\eta^2$.
:::
:::::

## PERMANOVA's One Real Assumption {.tight-code}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Equal dispersion

- A significant PERMANOVA means groups differ in **centroid** (location) *or* merely in **spread** (dispersion).
- `betadisper()` tells them apart.

```{r betadisper}
#| echo: true
#| class-output: tight-code
disp <- betadisper(
  vegdist(darl_scaled, method = "euclidean"),
  darlingtonia$site)

anova(disp)
```
:::

:::: {.column width="50%"}
### Reading the two together

- **Significant PERMANOVA + non-significant dispersion** → groups genuinely sit in different places. Clean result.
- **Both significant** → the location difference may be partly a spread difference. Say so.

```{r disp_means}
#| echo: true
round(tapply(disp$distances,
             darlingtonia$site, mean), 2)
```

- **Here both are significant**: LEH is the most variable. The site effect is strong enough (R² = 0.25) that it is not *only* dispersion — but an honest write-up mentions it.

::: callout-note
Week 15 develops PERMANOVA and ANOSIM in full on the Doubs data.
:::
::::
::::::

## Part 8 · Choosing a Method and Wrapping Up {.divider}

## A Decision Guide

::: compact-table
| Your data | Your question | Use |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Continuous traits, correlated, few zeros | What are the main axes of variation? | **PCA** (week 14) |
| Species counts, many zeros | How do communities arrange along a gradient? | **NMDS** (week 15) |
| Any dissimilarity matrix | Which objects group together? | **Cluster analysis** (week 15) |
| Any dissimilarity matrix | Do my groups differ? | **PERMANOVA / ANOSIM** (week 15) |
| Continuous, multivariate normal | Do groups differ, parametrically? | **MANOVA** |
| Categorical variables | Same questions, categorical data | **CA / MCA** |
:::

- Two questions settle almost every case:
  1.  **What kind of data is it?** → fixes the distance metric.
  2.  **Description or test?** → fixes ordination vs. PERMANOVA.

## Assumptions and Things That Go Wrong

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Check before you ordinate

- **Sample size**: at least 3× as many objects as variables; 50+ is comfortable. We have `r nrow(darlingtonia)` plants and `r ncol(darl_numeric)` variables.
- **Correlation**: if nothing correlates, PCA has nothing to collapse. `KMO()` gives a sampling-adequacy score; **ours is `r round(psych::KMO(cor(darl_numeric))$MSA, 2)`** (\> 0.6 acceptable, \> 0.8 good).
- **Linearity**: eigen methods see only linear relationships.
- **Outliers**: one extreme object can define an entire component.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Common mistakes

- ❌ Not standardizing variables with different units
- ❌ Euclidean distance on species counts
- ❌ Reading meaning into a sign flip
- ❌ Interpreting components that explain 3% of the variance
- ❌ Quoting "% variance explained" for an NMDS — it has none
- ❌ Calling a significant PERMANOVA a centroid difference without checking dispersion
- ❌ Treating an exploratory ordination as a confirmatory test
:::
:::::

## Reporting Multivariate Results

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
### Methods

> "Ten morphological and biomass variables measured on `r nrow(darlingtonia)` *Darlingtonia californica* plants from four sites were standardized to zero mean and unit variance and subjected to principal component analysis (`prcomp()`, R `r getRversion()`). Components with eigenvalues \> 1 were retained. Site differences were tested with PERMANOVA on Euclidean distances (`vegan::adonis2()`, 999 permutations), with homogeneity of multivariate dispersion checked using `betadisper()`."
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### Results — always state

1.  **% variance** for every component you interpret
2.  **Loadings** for the retained components
3.  The **biological reading** of each axis, sign resolved
4.  The **test** result with its dispersion check

### Never report

- All 10 components when 3 are meaningful
- Loadings below \|0.3\|
- Raw eigenvalues in place of percentages
- Every individual score
:::
:::::

## Summary

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
### What we did today

- **Standardized** 10 variables onto a common footing, because units are not biology.
- Built a **dissimilarity matrix** and learned that the choice of metric — Euclidean, Manhattan, Bray–Curtis, Jaccard — *is* the modelling decision.
- Saw the **map of ordination methods** and where each one lives in this course.
- Ran a PCA: 10 variables → **`r round(sum(prop_var[1:3])*100, 1)`% of the variation in three interpretable axes** (size, tube girth, wings).
- Ran an NMDS on fish counts and recovered a river gradient at stress = `r round(nmds$stress, 3)`.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### What to carry forward

- The **distance matrix is the hub**. Everything downstream reads from it.
- **Component signs are arbitrary** — translate into biology before you write a sentence.
- Ordination **describes**; PERMANOVA **tests**. Do not confuse them.
- **Next week**: what `prcomp()` is actually solving — eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and PCA in full.
- **Week 15**: NMDS, cluster analysis, PERMANOVA and ANOSIM in full.
:::
:::::

## Readings

- **Gotelli & Ellison**, *A Primer of Ecological Statistics*, **Ch. 12** — The Analysis of Multivariate Data
- **Quinn & Keough**, *Experimental Design and Data Analysis for Biologists*, **Ch. 15** (introduction to multivariate analyses) and **Ch. 16** (multivariate analysis of variance and discriminant analysis)
- Whitlock & Schluter does not cover multivariate methods.

### Data sources

- **Darlingtonia**: Ellison, A.M. & Farnsworth, E.J. — cobra lily morphology from four sites in the Siskiyou Mountains, Oregon; distributed with Gotelli & Ellison.
- **Doubs River fish**: Verneaux, J. (1973), as distributed in Borcard, Gillet & Legendre, *Numerical Ecology with R*.
